stories.headline: Trump arrives in China for historic summit with Xi and Putin

claims.text: President Trump arrived in Shenzhen, China on Wednesday for the APEC summit.
Xi Jinping personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac.
Xi Jinping's greeting of Trump reciprocated Trump's September greeting of Xi at Joint Base Andrews.
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in Shenzhen earlier Wednesday.
Putin was greeted by senior CCP official Cai Qi rather than Xi personally.
Putin held about two hours of talks with Xi before Trump's arrival.
Trump and Putin exchanged greetings at a reception Wednesday evening.
This was their first in-person contact since the August 2025 Alaska talks on Ukraine.
The August 2025 Alaska talks on Ukraine did not produce a breakthrough.
A U.S.-China-Russia trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin is scheduled for Thursday.
The trilateral meeting is described as the first such three-way in-person meeting.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said no more than an hour has been allocated for the trilateral meeting.
A separate one-on-one Trump-Putin meeting is also scheduled for Thursday.
The one-on-one meeting was confirmed by a U.S. official.
Potential topics across the meetings include the Ukraine war, nuclear weapons/proliferation, trade and artificial intelligence.
A senior U.S. official said before the trip that no formal denuclearization agreement is expected from the trilateral meeting.
The senior U.S. official called the trilateral meeting an 'entry point' and 'first conversation.'
During Trump's trip, technical outages affecting Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase and the NSA's communications network occurred in the U.S.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was 'zero' evidence the outages were connected to foreign actors.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was recently removed after admitting to an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleged was a Chinese agent.
China has denied the claim that the woman was a Chinese agent.

The Shenzhen summit is the first time the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia have met together in person.

Analysts and U.S. officials have tempered expectations, framing the trilateral session as a preliminary conversation rather than a venue for substantive agreements on Ukraine or nuclear arms.

ladder.analysis: The Shenzhen summit marks the first in-person meeting between Trump and Putin since their inconclusive Alaska talks, and the first time the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia have met together in person — an unprecedented diplomatic configuration given China and Russia's status as America's principal geopolitical rivals. The choreography carries its own significance: Xi's tarmac greeting of Trump, mirroring Trump's earlier welcome of Xi in Washington, signals Beijing's interest in maintaining cordial relations even as trade tensions, AI competition and the Nvidia-linked espionage allegation complicate the relationship. Analysts and U.S. officials have tempered expectations, framing the trilateral session — limited to roughly an hour, per the Kremlin — as a preliminary conversation rather than a venue for substantive agreements on Ukraine or nuclear arms. Concurrent U.S. tech outages, while described by officials as unconnected incidents tied to routine security patching, created a backdrop of uncertainty just as Trump sought to project American strength and technological leadership abroad.
ladder.steelman: Across all coverage, the consistent throughline is a gap between the summit's historic optics — an unprecedented three-way meeting and elaborate diplomatic choreography — and the modest, explicitly-acknowledged expectations for substantive outcomes, with even U.S. officials calling it merely a 'first conversation.'
ladder.implications: Thursday's meetings will test whether personal diplomacy between Trump, Xi and Putin can translate into movement on Ukraine, nuclear arms control or trade, though officials on multiple sides have downplayed the odds of a formal breakthrough. Ukrainian President Zelensky's concern about being excluded from any Ukraine-related discussions, along with unresolved questions about AI competition and chip access highlighted by the Nvidia episode, suggest that outcomes from Shenzhen will likely be assessed less by immediate agreements than by their effect on the trajectory of U.S. relations with both Beijing and Moscow in the months ahead.

stories.headline: Nvidia scandal deepens: Pence says Lutnick 'may need to go'; Nvidia won't reinstate Huang

claims.text: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman U.S. intelligence reports allege has ties to China's Ministry of State Security.
Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said the board 'does not intend to reinstate' Huang, after Huang said he would be 'honoured' to return as CEO.

Interim CEO Colette Kress said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper-based (H200) chips to China, without detailing why.
The Trump administration this week imposed new export restrictions on Chinese firms accessing advanced U.S. chips via third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil.
Former Vice President Mike Pence said on CNN's 'The Source' that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick 'may need to go' over his handling of Nvidia's China chip sales and the alleged honey-trap matter.

The controversy sits at the intersection of corporate governance, U.S.-China tech rivalry, and domestic political accountability. Nvidia's advanced chips, especially the H200, have been central to a years-long debate over whether exporting cutting-edge AI hardware to China strengthens its military and surveillance capacity or merely cedes commercial ground to Chinese rivals. The Trump administration's 2025 decision to allow H200 sales was seen as a rare thaw in that standoff, making Huang's ouster over an alleged espionage-linked affair — and Beijing's furious denials — politically combustible just as new export curbs were announced and a Trump-Xi summit approached.

For Nvidia, the business fundamentals remain strong: record sales and profits suggest the company's momentum is not immediately dependent on Huang personally, even as the board faces pressure over succession and the China-exposure fallout. For Washington, the episode has reopened bipartisan scrutiny of how export policy was set and enforced, with questions about oversight (Commerce Secretary Lutnick) and about the administration's broader posture toward China converging on a single scandal just as high-stakes diplomacy with Beijing unfolds in Shenzhen.

ladder.implications: The scandal's immediate fallout — Nvidia's refusal to reinstate Huang, halted Hopper shipments to China, and new third-country export restrictions — will test whether the Trump-Xi summit can stay focused on trade rather than security disputes, while in Washington, bipartisan criticism of Commerce Secretary Lutnick and the administration's chip-export oversight could prompt congressional hearings or further legislative restrictions on AI chip sales to China.

stories.headline: Trump meets Xi and Putin at APEC summit in China
body: US President Donald Trump shook hands and exchanged greetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin before a group photo at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. Xi Jinping personally greeted Trump on the airport tarmac, reciprocating the welcome Trump extended to Xi during his visit to the US in September. A trilateral meeting among the three leaders is scheduled for Thursday and is expected to last less than one hour, according to Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov. The Associated Press, citing an anonymous US official, reported that Trump also plans to hold a separate bilateral meeting with Putin on Thursday, which would be their first since talks in Alaska in 2025 failed to reach a deal on the war in Ukraine.

Before arriving in China, Trump was in Manila, where he met with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang presidential palace. During a meeting ahead of lunch, Marcos revealed he had arranged for fried chicken from the Filipino fast-food chain Jollibee to be delivered to the US delegation as a late-night snack, praising Trump for 'working very hard.' Trump told Marcos he knew his 'parents very well' and praised the palace, saying, 'I love what you’ve done here.' Trump also announced that the US had concluded a 'very big trade deal' with the Philippines, though he provided no details and Manila did not announce any agreement.

Xi Jinping told Trump he hoped their talks would help advance a 'constructive, strategic and stable relationship' between China and the US, based on 'respect, fairness and reciprocity,' according to China’s state news agency Xinhua. Xi also recalled Trump’s personal welcome at the airport during his visit to the US in September, saying China’s own welcome reflected its tradition of reciprocity. Earlier, Xi met with Putin and was quoted by Chinese state media as saying China-Russia relations are 'unshaken by storms and steady as a mountain,' setting 'an example of a new type of major-country relationship.'

On the sidelines of the summit, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney challenged Putin’s earlier assertion that sanctions no longer work, telling reporters: 'Mr Putin can ask his financial institutions, he can ask his oligarch friends, he can ask his hockey players whether or not sanctions are a thing of the past. I think he’ll find out that they’re very real, they’re biting.' Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum went viral on Chinese social media for taking an economy flight to the summit, while Trump’s visit came as a series of technical outages back in the US left his administration scrambling to calm the public. Trump had been nonchalant about the outages, saying from Manila, 'It’s fine,' and suggesting it was a consequence of being a nation that is 'big and powerful.'

The APEC summit in Shenzhen, China’s tech hub, opened with Xi calling for freer trade and greater cooperation on artificial intelligence. Trump arrived seeking to reinforce America’s status as the world’s leading technology power. It remains unclear whether North Korean leader Kim Jong-un will attend the talks, though Trump has floated the possibility. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the president was willing to engage but did not confirm whether a meeting had been set.

stories.headline: Kuwait and Bahrain repel Iranian attacks after US strike on Qeshm Island
body: Kuwait and Bahrain said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight, marking the first such assault on Kuwait in more than two months and the fourth on Bahrain in six days. The attacks came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials. The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem Air Base, which hosts US forces. Kuwaiti authorities reported no casualties or damage. Bahrain's military said its air defence systems had 'intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks.'

The US said it carried out the strike on Qeshm Island 'with precision munitions' in response to Iranian 'aggression targeting US personnel and assets,' specifically an earlier Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain. Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they caused no damage to infrastructure. Iran's army commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned that if 'the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations.'

In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated, and 11 were receiving medical care. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, causing a fire that was extinguished. Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an 'authorised route.'

The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Since then, Iran has retaliated by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and has attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass. At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the strait was effectively closed due to Iranian attacks and a US naval blockade. A preliminary US-Iran agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait collapsed in June after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

The recent exchanges of fire and deadlock in negotiations have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war. Kuwait's foreign ministry condemned the drone attacks, saying they 'flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law.' Qatar, which has mediated stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, called the attacks 'a dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions.' Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry condemned the attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain 'in the strongest terms' and denounced the attack on the UAE tanker. Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks reveal 'a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation.'

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold first trilateral meeting at APEC summit
body: The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in Shenzhen, China. US President Donald Trump will also hold separate talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering.

Experts do not expect breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further are seen as more realistic shared objectives. Patricia M. Kim of the Brookings Institution said neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda. Jia Hui Tee of the Hinrich Foundation noted that reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side could be an easy win, though an indicative implementation timeline has not been set. She added that China would likely be cautious with commitments given Trump's weaker domestic position after Republican losses in the midterm elections.

Zhang Lun of CY Cergy Paris University said Trump faces pressure at home from becoming a lame-duck president after the midterms, and abroad from strained ties with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, and difficulties in the Iran war. Zhang argued these factors have reduced America's leverage and made Trump more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation. Another meeting between Trump and Xi is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, allowing contentious issues to be pushed to a later date.

Russia hopes the trilateral talks will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow. Yun Sun of the Stimson Center said Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to negotiate, which could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine. Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks, while Beijing wants the optics of hosting the historic meeting. Alicja Bachulska of the European Council on Foreign Relations said Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached, predicting each leader will restate their positions rather than produce real solutions.

On Ukraine, Michael Kimmage of the Kennan Institute said China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively ending the war, as Russia remains an important energy source and diplomatic partner. Zhang Lun believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing but not support it so openly that it alienates Europe, and does not want Ukraine to be defeated because that would reduce Russia's dependence on China. He expects China to wait for a more favorable moment to potentially step in as a neutral mediator.

On Iran, W.A. Figueroa of the University of Groningen said there is little indication of real cooperation between China and the US. The two countries share some interests, including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation, but China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced sanctions and military force. Figueroa noted that China continues to provide Iran with financial support through purchases of Iranian oil and has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi and Putin hold rare trilateral meeting at APEC in Shenzhen
body: U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a trilateral meeting Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, according to Beijing's official confirmation of the event billed as the 'China-Russia-U.S. Summit.' The meeting marked the first-ever gathering of the three leaders, though expectations for substantive breakthroughs were low given limited time for dialogue.

The trilateral encounter came after Xi hosted a welcome banquet Wednesday evening where Trump and Putin were seated just a few spots apart. Xi raised a toast, saying in Mandarin, 'At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results,' according to a CNBC translation. Trump did not deliver a toast of his own.

U.S. officials said ahead of the summit that Trump did not plan to raise allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days. Instead, talks were expected to focus on implementing the existing trade agreement between the two countries. The U.S. and China in September agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from the other country, though no effective date was specified. China has said it would only increase purchases of U.S. agricultural products if those tariffs were reduced.

The APEC summit comes amid heightened geopolitical tensions. China's relations with Japan have escalated since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's comments last November indicating Tokyo would support Taiwan if seriously threatened by Beijing's military. Takaichi is attending the summit in her first trip to China as prime minister. The Russia-Ukraine war continues to pressure global energy prices, and the Iran war is now in its ninth month. 'Across Asia, governments under mounting pressure to pick a side will be watching Shenzhen for signs of how much room they still have to maneuver,' said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. 'Most have little appetite for a region split into two technology camps.'

Tech issues were a central focus of the summit. Nvidia released quarterly results Wednesday morning Beijing time, boosting its outlook and sending shares higher in extended trading, following the resignation of founder Jensen Huang amid scrutiny of the company's China chip sales. Shenzhen-based Tencent is set to report quarterly earnings Wednesday evening. U.S.-based AI giant Anthropic is pricing its initial public offering this week, expected to list on the Nasdaq Thursday Nov. 19. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen but was not seen at the Wednesday evening banquet.

The APEC host city, Shenzhen, known as one of China's 'Silicon Valleys' and home to Huawei and BYD, is using the event to showcase local robotics startups. The summit also includes the APEC CEO Summit, where Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said 'the entire multilateral framework needs to change,' praising China's recognition of smaller countries. Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader took the stage at the opening event; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon. Vietnam, which is hosting next year's APEC meetings, had its president meet with Xi earlier in the week.

stories.headline: New U.S. rules threaten Southeast Asia data center boom fueled by Chinese demand
body: New U.S. export rules could slow Southeast Asia's data center boom by tightening access to advanced AI chips and targeting the region's role in providing computing power to Chinese companies. According to an interim rule released Monday by the Commerce Department, data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia will need a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including those from Nvidia. Facilities already serving large Chinese customers will have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions.

The region has seen a surge in data center construction to house the semiconductors needed to train and develop artificial intelligence models. U.S. restrictions on China's access to Nvidia's most advanced chips have pushed Chinese technology firms, including Alibaba Group and ByteDance, to rent computing capacity in overseas data centers. About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by the end of 2026, according to October estimates by the Institute for Progress, a Washington-based think tank.

The new restrictions will likely make building and operating these data centers "slower and costlier," said Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. The rules could undercut the business model of neoclouds — newer cloud providers built around AI computing — in the region, she said. Operators are likely to face more rigorous regulatory and national security requirements, said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. Greater scrutiny over investment into these projects could also weigh on Asian economies that have benefited heavily from the region's data center build-out.

Malaysia stands to lose the most from the new restrictions, analysts say, given the scale of capacity being built in Johor and the sector's reliance on Chinese customers. More than half of Malaysia's data center capacity is in colocation facilities with Chinese firms accounting for "a sizeable share of these workloads," said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics. Restricting access to overseas cloud facilities would weaken the commercial case for further expansion and ultimately weigh on investment from both Chinese and U.S. companies, Fahy said. "Any resulting slowdown in investment would add to the drag from an anticipated cooling in the global AI export cycle," she said, potentially knocking 0.2 percentage points off Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028. Malaysian data centers that rely heavily on Chinese customers, particularly those built for AI training, may struggle to lease space and fill capacity, and could be left with idle power, Goldman Sachs analysts wrote.

Thailand, which has more than 60 data centers operating and about 30 under construction, is also bracing for tighter scrutiny. Thailand's vice minister for commerce, Kirida Bhaopichitr, told CNBC on Sunday that the country would scrutinize data centers importing high-end chips and "crack down" on those that re-export them to third countries. New projects that fail to secure U.S. approval for advanced chips may "not be able to complete construction," the vice minister said, though existing facilities providing AI services could be less affected. Governments in the region have signaled compliance with the U.S. requirements. Malaysia's investment, trade and industry minister, Johari Abdul Ghani, said Tuesday, "If you want to be in the game, you have to follow U.S. regulations." Singapore, meanwhile, has said it plans to negotiate "trusted access" to advanced AI chips for its companies.

The rule exempts U.S.-headquartered companies, leaving a narrow path for Chinese firms to keep renting advanced computing power from U.S. cloud giants, analysts said, though those providers may become more cautious about leasing to Chinese customers. "Potentially, U.S. firms may receive an advantage," said Chong. "There is a significant risk that Chinese companies will pivot from renting compute from data centers in Southeast Asia to renting compute from data centers in Virginia," said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former National Security Council official. He urged Washington to close that loophole before it is exploited. Bhattacharya said some high-end capacity may also shift to Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, though constraints on power and land may restrain how much those markets can absorb. Chinese technology companies have already begun looking for alternative sources of computing power outside of Southeast Asia. CNBC reported earlier this month that Chinese developer Moonshot AI tried to access Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. Oracle canceled a multibillion-dollar chip-leasing agreement with Tencent in early November that would have given the Chinese company access to about 100,000 advanced AI chips, according to the Financial Times, bowing to pressure from U.S. administration officials.

stories.headline: Zverev to defend himself against fresh lawsuit over domestic abuse trial outcome
body: Lawyers for world number one Alexander Zverev say he will defend himself against a lawsuit that alleges he misrepresented the outcome of his domestic abuse trial. Former partner Brenda Patea is seeking damages and an injunction to prevent him from making similar comments in the future.

In October 2023, Zverev was issued a penalty order for bodily harm against Patea, with whom he has a daughter. He contested the order, having always denied the charges, and a public trial was underway in Berlin in June 2024 when the court terminated the proceedings. The court told the BBC: 'The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence. One decisive factor for the decision was that the witness has expressed her wish to end the trial. The defendant agreed to the termination of the case.' The court said there had been a separate settlement between Zverev and Patea.

In September, lawyers for Patea filed a civil complaint in Berlin about an interview Zverev gave to French newspaper L'Equipe in June, the day after he won his first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros. According to the complaint, L'Equipe reported that Zverev allegedly said 'my innocence has been proven'. The lawsuit asks that Zverev be ordered 'on pain of a fine of up to 250,000 euros (£209,000)' not to repeat the claim, and also seeks damages for the impact these statements have made on Patea.

Patea's lawyer, Michael Scheele, told BBC Sport: 'He was not found guilty, but he was not acquitted and they signed an agreement in which he committed not to talk about this case any more. Instead he has said that it has been proven that he was not guilty. It's simply false.' Scheele added: 'She doesn't want this to be repeated, because she's a content creator, an influencer, and she was accused of trying to make money, which was not true. If that had been the case, she would have asked in that [original] agreement to be compensated. He made a payment for the daughter, but nothing for her. She did not get any money.'

Zverev is being represented by Berlin law firm Schertz Bergmann, which said: 'Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law. Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. He is fully entitled to hold and express this view. The criminal proceedings were discontinued without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected.'

The out-of-court settlement in Berlin in June 2024 came on the day Zverev reached the French Open final for the first time. In a subsequent news conference, he was asked by BBC Sport whether he had any reservations about missing the opportunity to clear his name entirely. Zverev replied: 'That's what dropping the case is. That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty. I don't know what translations you have, but that's what it means. Done. We move on. I never ever want to hear another question about the subject again. That goes out to everybody.'

stories.headline: SEC frustration over LSU's RJ Luis could lead to boycotts if Will Wade puts ex-St. John's star on court
body: With the college basketball season underway, the most pressing question in the SEC is not about Florida's national standing or Kentucky's early struggles, but whether LSU will put RJ Luis on the floor. The Tigers face Louisiana Monroe on Wednesday night, and if Luis — who has not played college basketball since March 2025 — steps onto the court in LSU threads, the conference could face a crisis that has been building for weeks.

On Nov. 13, Baton Rouge-based Judge Will Jorden granted Luis a preliminary injunction that bars the SEC from punishing LSU or Luis if the school rosters the 24-year-old. The SEC responded days later by saying it would abide by the injunction while it remains in place and would not impose penalties or fines if LSU places Luis on its roster. LSU President Wade Rousse then issued a statement Tuesday saying the school is committed to compliance with NCAA and SEC rules but equally committed to obeying Louisiana courts, adding that LSU will act in accordance with the court order.

The SEC quickly pushed back, calling LSU's decision to rely on its own interpretation of the court order inconsistent with the expectations of SEC membership and a deeply concerning and disappointing development. The conference had previously voted in a penalty structure for any program that rosters or plays someone who signed a professional contract after previously being enrolled in college: a half-season suspension for the head coach, revocation of SEC voting privileges for the school, a 50% fine of the sport's fiscal-year operating budget, and leeway for the commissioner to enact additional penalties. However, the SEC cannot enforce those penalties while the injunction stands.

Sources told CBS Sports that the idea of at least some SEC schools boycotting games against LSU has been discussed among athletic directors and presidents. One SEC source said it could lead to all sorts of negative ramifications, including boycotts, and that it is not hyperbole to say boycotts will happen. Another source noted that it is 15 to 1 on this deal and that if LSU rosters a former NBA player, that will lead to activity in the federal case pending in Alabama between the conference and LSU over the school's attempt to roster two football players cut from NFL training camps. A similar maelstrom surrounded Texas Tech in June after quarterback Brendan Sorsby's gambling activity prompted multiple schools to threaten boycotts.

The situation has drawn comparisons to Alabama's attempt to keep Charles Bediako on its roster in early 2026, which required SEC litigation and went to Alabama's Supreme Court. Multiple SEC coaches told CBS Sports they hope Commissioner Greg Sankey will severely punish LSU if it plays Luis for even one game, citing inconsistent eligibility rulings across the league — Kentucky had to abandon its quest for Mark Mitchell (now at Missouri) due to a calendar technicality, Missouri's CJ Gunn was ruled ineligible based on the SEC's interpretation of being a paid professional, and Auburn brought in a grad transfer from Stanford who remains ineligible after a recent rule change. Luis, meanwhile, is one yes away from seeing the floor, and he even played in preseason games, which one source said makes this worse than the Bediako case.

If LSU goes through with playing Luis, battle lines will be drawn and the war will truly begin. The SEC has previously invoked the threat of expulsion against LSU over the football player dispute, and that threat remains, however remote. One source said votes can be had to change any number of conference rules, including forfeiture policy for football games. For now, the conference is complying with the court order, but the possibility of boycotts — and the broader legal and political fallout — hangs over every decision LSU makes in the coming days.

stories.headline: U.S. loses measles elimination status as outbreaks surge
body: International health officials announced Tuesday that the United States has lost its measles elimination status, a widely expected but deeply symbolic setback that formalizes what public health departments have been seeing on the ground for years. The decision came after a meeting of a committee of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional body of the World Health Organization. The designation marks the first time since 2000, when U.S. health authorities declared measles eliminated, that the country has been found to have sustained transmission of the virus for at least 12 months. “Losing measles elimination status is a tragic loss for our country,” said Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer for the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials. “Measles has taken a hold in our country.”

This year, the U.S. has reported more than 5,000 measles cases — the highest since 1991 and widely believed to be an undercount. Last year’s total of 2,289 cases was also the highest since 1991. The overwhelming majority of infections — 96% — are in unvaccinated people or those whose vaccination status is unknown. The U.S. has seen 10 measles-associated deaths this year, according to state data, though the CDC’s website currently lists six deaths. New York and Wisconsin recently reported their first measles deaths in at least 30 years. Last year, there were three measles deaths. Doctors are also reporting an increase in complications from measles infections in pregnancy, both maternal and neonatal.

Measles elimination status is conferred when a country prevents persistent spread of the virus. Cases can still occur when people infected abroad import the virus, and limited transmission can take place from those infected people. But if those chains of spread are not stopped within a year, measles is considered endemic again. “Elimination must be continuously protected,” PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa said at a news briefing. The PAHO commission’s review focused on a period starting in January 2025 and depended on establishing that a series of cases continued for at least 12 months. “It is unconscionable that we have this amount of measles,” said Noel Brewer, a public health expert at the University of North Carolina who chairs the group providing data on the U.S. measles landscape to PAHO. “We need a plan,” Brewer said. “The United States is no longer a safe place for children with respect to measles.”

The U.S.’s susceptibility to measles has been building for years. Vaccination rates within certain regions and communities have slipped due to a rise in vaccine skepticism, the spread of misinformation online, failures of public health campaigns, or the perception that measles does not pose a threat. While vaccine coverage of 95% of people is considered sufficient to keep a lid on measles transmission, the vaccination rate for kindergarteners has dropped below 90% in nearly 20 states. Adults have made up sizable portions of infections in some recent case clusters, a sign that it is not just a retrenchment of parents not immunizing their children. “The fact that the flag was raised, and it was not heeded, is to me the most alarming thing,” said Maia Majumder, a computational epidemiologist at Boston Children’s Hospital, who co-authored a Lancet paper in May about the at-risk elimination designation.

The announcement could have political ramifications, with resurgent Democrats attacking the Trump administration — in particular, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — for not responding forcefully to recent outbreaks and for mixed messaging around the benefits of vaccination. Kennedy has at times acknowledged that the best way to prevent measles is the MMR shot, including in a social media post Tuesday, but he also has a long history of attacking vaccines with false arguments. As health secretary, he has downplayed the severity of outbreaks, overstated the risks of the vaccine, and pointed to unproven treatments. In a statement Tuesday, CDC Director Erica Schwartz said the U.S. is “focused on stopping outbreaks.” “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does,” she said, adding that the CDC has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach affected communities. Sen. Michael Bennet (D-Colo.) called on Schwartz to resign after the PAHO decision. Dr. Ashish Jha, a senior fellow at Harvard’s Belfer Center and former White House coronavirus czar, told NPR that the backsliding “did not begin under this administration, but it has gotten dramatically worse under this administration.” He added, “There is no question in my mind that Secretary Kennedy has done a completely inadequate job of addressing this problem.”

stories.headline: Discovery reveals key obstacle to room-temperature superconductors
body: Researchers from Utrecht University, Leiden University, and the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich have discovered that one of the two essential conditions for superconductivity can exist at room temperature, narrowing the search for materials that could conduct electricity without resistance. The findings, published November 18, 2026 in the journal Science, show that electrons can form stable pairs—known as Cooper pairs—at temperatures far higher than previously understood, but that a second condition, phase coherence, remains the bottleneck preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

Superconductivity allows electrical current to flow with zero resistance, which could enable technologies such as magnetically levitated trains, lossless energy storage, and more efficient quantum computers. However, most superconductors require extreme cooling to approximately -260°C using liquid helium, making widespread use costly. In the mid-1980s, a new class of materials was discovered that could superconduct at around -173°C, but the mechanism behind this high-temperature superconductivity has remained a mystery. "We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," said Ingmar Swart, one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

Superconductivity depends on two processes: electrons must first join into Cooper pairs, and then those pairs must move in a coordinated quantum state called phase coherence. In conventional superconductors, both conditions emerge at the same temperature. The new study reveals that in high-temperature superconductors, electron pairing can occur at temperatures substantially higher than the temperature at which superconductivity itself appears—and that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature. "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," Swart said. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

The team made the discovery using specialized measurement equipment that could distinguish electrical current carried by individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. By separating these contributions, the researchers identified that while electron pairing is possible at room temperature, achieving and maintaining phase coherence remains the critical challenge. "If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures," Swart added. He plans to investigate this process in future research.

The findings do not mean room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved, but they demonstrate that one essential ingredient can survive under everyday conditions. "This is really good news," Swart said. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether." The journal reference is: Jiasen Niu et al., "Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor," Science 394 (6824): 682 (2026), DOI: 10.1126/science.adt3444.

stories.headline: First direct observation of a star engulfed by a giant star
body: Astronomers have reported the first direct detection of a star being engulfed by a giant companion, a long-predicted but elusive event known as the common-envelope phase. The observation, published in Nature by Karambelkar and colleagues, captures a moment when a star in its giant phase swells and swallows a neighbouring star, placing the smaller object inside the larger one.

The common-envelope phase occurs when a star expands dramatically toward the end of its life, entering what is known as the giant phase. Because most stars are thought to host orbiting companions—such as planets, other stars, or black holes—the expanding giant can engulf a nearby companion. Despite theoretical expectations that this process should be widespread in stellar evolution, direct observations have been extraordinarily difficult to obtain until now.
The new study provides the first direct evidence of a star inside a giant star.

The discovery is detailed in a News and Views article in the same issue of Nature, which notes that the common-envelope phase has been predicted to be common but had remained observationally hidden. The authors of the News and Views piece highlight that Karambelkar et al. have finally captured this dramatic event directly.

stories.headline: Microsoft embeds Office apps inside Copilot, announces always-on agents
body: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced Tuesday at the company’s Ignite event that Word, Excel, and PowerPoint are now generally available inside Copilot, which he described as “the new OS for work.” The announcement inverts the traditional software model: instead of an application like Word being the primary tool with an assistant like Clippy to help use it, Microsoft envisions agents driving tasks while Office applications serve as plugin components. Users can now create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

The rollout marks a major step toward the Copilot redesign Microsoft first announced in September. Alongside the Office integration, Microsoft introduced Copilot Autopilot, a “persistent, proactive agent for personal productivity” that operates as a cloud-based autonomous AI agent. Unlike single-task assistants, Autopilot can be authorized to work across services like email and calendars and complete assigned tasks as part of its role. It will use usage-based billing via Copilot Credits, though final pricing has not been announced ahead of general availability.

Also announced as generally available was Microsoft IQ, an intelligence platform that houses Work IQ, a context layer that helps agents understand a company’s communications, relationships, and ongoing work. Nadella described Work IQ as perhaps a company’s most valuable database: “It has a deep understanding of the people, their relationships to other people, your emails, your meetings, chats, projects that make up all the fabric of work.” Whether companies allow autonomous agents access to internal documents and messaging data will be determined by their own internal IT review.

The new Copilot integrations are backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Nadella outlined the company’s vision for its new “frontier ecosystem,” with autonomous agents and new governance tools arriving alongside the Office integration. The announcements position Copilot as a central platform for work, with applications becoming components of the agent’s workflow.

stories.headline: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to critical acclaim
body: Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest installment in Rockstar Games' blockbuster franchise, was developed with a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development. The game reimagines the iconic Vice City as a grand, crude, satirical criminal playground, rendered with technical polish and an extraordinary level of detail. According to Ars Technica's review, the game's massive map spans more than six miles from the northern wilderness to the southern keys, requiring up to 10 minutes to traverse by vehicle.

The core innovation of GTA VI is its dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a young criminal couple whose relationship drives the story. Jason is an ex-military meathead with a dull, affect-free demeanor, while Lucia is a vivacious and amiable Latina eager to seize opportunities. The game's writing explores Lucia's underprivileged youth and strained family relationships, adding depth to her character. Their partnership is reinforced by a simple relationship simulation system—a "heart level" that rises or falls based on obvious choices—and the game frequently shifts perspective between the two, though the lack of a co-op mode for missions is noted as a baffling omission.

The review highlights the game's signature juxtaposition of over-the-top action and mundane domestic life. Explosive gunfights and high-speed chases are counterpointed by lightly interactive moments such as grilling burgers, playing fetch with a dog, or assembling Ikea-style furniture. This contrast lends a surreal hyperreality to Vice City, with emotional peaks and valleys stretching across a gargantuan amount of content. The shooting mechanics remain familiar—cover-based combat with relatively unintelligent enemies—while driving is described as significantly more exciting, with a wide variety of vehicles and traffic to navigate.

The main storyline is divided into two halves. The first half involves the pair running errands for a rogues' gallery of one-note criminal caricatures, which can feel repetitive. The back half focuses on integrating Jason and Lucia into a professional criminal ring, with missions that build on each other through undercover work, casing targets, and tense heists that best showcase the dual-protagonist system. Outside the core plot, many side missions make the protagonists feel like side characters in their own story, and even dozens of hours in, some missions still feel like tutorials for new systems.

The game's humor retains the sophomoric style that defined earlier entries, with extended bits about kinky sex and phallic imagery, though some side stories offer sharper satire of crypto bros and multi-level marketing schemes. The review notes that the game's takes on 'wokeness' feel dated, without much in the way of thought-provoking statements on society. Parents are warned that the game earns a hard "M for Mature" rating, reflecting how standards have shifted since the series' earlier controversies.

Despite these criticisms, Grand Theft Auto VI is praised as a technical marvel and a world players will want to inhabit long after the main story ends. Dozens of side activities—including drone racing, rally races, and meditation spots—offer distractions that improve character stats or simply exist to be experienced. The review concludes that the game's ability to balance its two sides—criminal bombast and domestic routine—makes it all the better, with the relationship between Jason and Lucia providing an emotional core that is easy to root for, even as they get away with murder.
